newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - gas oil threatens margins.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - gas oil threatens margins.

text.p: European oil products prices may be under threat from weaker gas oil this week but the lighter and the heavier products should provide support, traders said.
Buying of diesel and gasoline ahead of the U.K. government's November 26 budget, in which taxes on road fuels are expected to be raised, should add a layer of support to refining margins.
Outright gas oil prices have suffered from bearish news from the U.S., where latest data showed inventories recovered strongly from historically low levels.
Dealers said this tendency was also reflected in Europe after moves by refiners to boost output of middle distillates.
Gas oil stocks in the key ARA region rose by five percent week-on-week to around 1.7 million tonnes, according to latest data from industry sources.

Arriving arbitrage cargoes from across the Atlantic will further boost Europe's stocks position, with one dealer guessing these could push low sulphur diesel, currently bid at around $18 over November IPE, some $3 or $4 lower.
But with the arbitrage window now closed, the fall is not likely to be hard or sustained, traders said.
Jet fuel is set to maintain recent firmness on tight supply, traders said.

But European refiners' moves to boost gas oil output has a flip side too - reduced output of gasoline, which is expected to trade sideways to higher next week despite the normal fall in winter demand.
Continued buying into the Thames ahead of the U.K. budget should also keep gasoline steady relative to Brent.

As a result, the gasoline crack spread against crude oil should hold at $4 to $5 versus front month Brent, regardless of the volatility in the crude market."Personally for mogas I see flat to higher prices...$220 seems to be good support" for the Eurograde barges fob ARA, one trader said.
But another said refinery economics may also soon favour producing gasoline. "This market...is very nervous," he said.
Naphtha is tight and should stay firm this week. Good petrochemical demand and high freight rates have discouraged shipping cargoes from the Med to northwest Europe.
Fuel oil traders were alert to rumours swirling through the market about the possibility of new Russian export taxes.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who has previously signed any decrees relating to export taxes, has taken on some of President Boris Yeltsin's powers ahead of his imminent heart operation.

"I doubt Chernomyrdin will be thinking about fuel oil," one dealer said. Export volumes are set to fall sharply in any case, however, as winter sets and boosts local demand. European supply will shorten as a result.
In addition, ARA inventories, currently at around 350,000 tonnes, are little over half of last year's levels.
